title: 7 Signs You’re a Better Manager Than You Think
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain draws on more than twenty years of leading teams to argue that many signs of good management feel like failures in the moment. He begins with the irony that the worst manager he knew never wondered whether he was good, while the best asked constantly, and he treats self-doubt as evidence of care and growing competence. The remaining signs include a team that brings bad news early, people who disagree in the meeting rather than after it, work that runs smoothly while the manager is on leave, former reports who outgrow their manager, a willingness to change one's mind in front of the team, and noticing when someone is off before they say anything. Each sign comes with a concrete try-this practice. His conclusion is that the feeling of good management lags behind its results.
points: Self-doubt about managing well is recast as a sign of caring and of having learned enough to see how much remains.
Bad news reaches trusted managers first, so early warnings indicate psychological safety.
Open disagreement in meetings is healthier than silent nodding followed by hallway complaints, as the Abilene paradox illustrates.
A team that functions during a manager's vacation shows the manager built capability rather than dependence.
Changing your mind in front of the team teaches people to bring their best ideas instead of their safest.
quotes: Here’s an irony: the worst manager I ever worked for never wondered if he was a “good manager”, but the best one asked himself that question all the time.
Here’s what I’ve learned after 20+ years of leading teams: the signs that you’re doing well as a manager don’t always look “good” in the moment. In fact, some of them feel like failures.
Remember that bad news travels to the managers that people trust, and last to the ones they don’t.
In fact, I would actually worry if your team is nodding along in the meetings, and then complaining to you in the hallway conversation.

Many managers are wary of going on long vacations because they feel that “the team needed them.” But, in almost every case, the team didn’t need them. The team had just never been given the chance to prove that.
When you change your mind because someone on the team had a good argument, they learn that good ideas matter and that you care. They start bringing you their best ideas instead of the safest ones.
Here’s the irony: good management rarely feels “good” while you’re doing it. The feeling always shows up later in the results.
